name: Gliding / sliding cupping

lead: Gliding or sliding cupping is a version of cupping therapy where the skin is oiled and a cup creating mild suction is moved across it instead of staying in one spot. It is used in traditional Chinese medicine and in massage-style cupping on the back, limbs and sometimes the face.

Practitioners use it to relax muscle and stimulate skin circulation, which people associate with a refreshed look and less tension. A 2026 randomised trial tested sliding cupping against narrowband UVB in plaque psoriasis, which is a skin-condition application.

paras: A therapist applies oil, creates suction in a cup (by pump, flame or heat in traditional versions) and glides it over an area for roughly 10 to 20 minutes. Facial and body versions use smaller cups with lighter suction.

Cupping can leave circular marks or bruises, and fire cupping has caused burns. It may worsen eczema or psoriasis in some people, and people with heart conditions or high blood pressure are advised by some health ministries to be cautious.

angle.text: Practitioners say the suction lifts and mobilises skin and muscle, giving a massage effect and a flushed, refreshed look. The technique is also used on the body for tension relief.

lead: Gliding or sliding cupping is a type of cupping therapy in which oil is applied to the skin and the cup is moved across muscle rather than left in place. Wikipedia describes it as a form of fire cupping that uses oil to let the cups glide, and distinguishes it from stationary dry cupping and wet cupping [1]. Massage cupping, in which cups are moved over the back, chest or limbs for roughly 10 to 20 minutes, is a related approach [1].

People use it as a massage-like treatment for muscle tension and skin circulation. Its cosmetic relevance comes mainly through the facial cupping trend, in which small cups are glided over the face with oil. Research on the method includes a 2026 randomised trial in plaque psoriasis [2], while broader reviews of cupping describe the evidence as low in quality [1].

paras: In sliding cupping, the practitioner applies oil, creates suction inside a glass, bamboo or silicone cup, and moves the cup across the skin. Traditional versions create suction with heat from a flame, while modern ones often use a pump [1]. Practitioners describe the technique as stimulating circulation and relieving muscle tightness, in line with traditional Chinese medicine ideas of removing stagnation and improving qi flow [1].

A 2026 randomised trial published in Medicine enrolled 60 patients with plaque psoriasis and tested whether sliding cupping was non-inferior to narrowband UVB phototherapy [2]. Broader reviews of cupping report poor study quality and inconsistent blinding, with low to moderate evidence for musculoskeletal pain that may not differ from placebo [1].

Cupping causes capillaries under the skin to break, leaving circular bruises or petechiae. Reported adverse effects include burns, scarring, discoloration, ulcers and possible worsening of eczema or psoriasis, with higher risk for fire and wet cupping [1].
